findings.claim: Practice question 3 is labelled '2 marks — State / Give' ('Give two contrasting Buddhist beliefs about the purpose of meditation'), with a 2-mark key.
findings.truth: This paper sets two five-part questions per religion of 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12 marks. There is no 2-mark part. Re-cast as the 4-mark Explain and re-size the key to 2 marks per belief.

findings.claim: Practice question 3 is labelled '2 marks — State / Give' ('Give two differences between the way Wesak and Parinirvana Day are observed by Buddhists').
findings.truth: No 2-mark part exists on this paper (1, 1, 4, 6, 12). Re-cast as the 4-mark Explain and re-size the key.

findings.claim: Practice question 3 is labelled '2 marks — State / Give' ('Give two ways in which a lay Buddhist might express the quality of karuna').
findings.truth: No 2-mark part exists on this paper (1, 1, 4, 6, 12). Re-cast as the 4-mark Explain and re-size the key.

findings.claim: Both 4-mark keys read '2 marks per item: 1 mark for naming the item; 2 marks for explaining what it represents' - which reads as 3 marks inside a 2-mark slot.
findings.truth: A 4-mark part gives 2 marks per item on a 1-2 scale: 1 mark for naming, 2 marks for naming and explaining. Recomputation: 2 items x 2 marks = 4.
findings.evidence: recomputation against the 4-mark part in specs/aqa/religious-studies-8062-8062.md line 1832

findings.claim: The 4-mark key reads '2 marks per practice: 1 mark for naming the practice; 2 marks for explaining its significance'.
findings.truth: Same arithmetic defect as F4; the key is a 1-2 scale, not 1 plus 2.

findings.claim: The 6-mark key says making offerings and bowing 'counteract the Three Poisons (greed and pride)'.
findings.truth: The Three Poisons are ignorance, greed and hate. Pride is not one of them. A student repeating this loses the mark on a named spec item.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/religious-studies-8062-8062.md: 'the Three Poisons, ignorance, greed and hate'; lesson 2 of this unit states the list correctly

findings.claim: The 6-mark key cites 'the Dhammapada 190-191 on the samadhi dimension of the path' and says the verses 'describe the Threefold Way of sila, samadhi and panna as the path to nibbana'.
findings.truth: Dhammapada 190-191 is about going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha and thereby seeing the Four Noble Truths, the last of which is the Noble Eightfold Path. The verses say nothing about sila, samadhi and panna. This is the prescribed text named in the spec, so the misattribution is exam-critical.
findings.evidence: accesstoinsight.org Dhammapada ch.14 vv.190-191 (Buddharakkhita); spec attaches Dhammapada 190-191 to the Eightfold Path bullet

findings.claim: Four further citations of the same prescribed text: 'Dhammapada 190-191 on sila as part of the Threefold Way'; 'the Dhammapada 190-191 teaches that the Eightfold Path operates as sila, samadhi and panna'; 'Dhammapada 190-191 on sila'; 'The Dhammapada 190-191 grounds the Eightfold Path in the Threefold Way'. The exam tip also calls the verses 'a strong source for the ethical dimension of the path'.
findings.truth: The verses cover the Three Refuges, the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path. They are not a source on sila or on the Threefold Way analysis. Corrected wording states what the verses actually say and keeps the Threefold Way as a separate claim.

findings.claim: 'Zen is sometimes called the “silent illumination” school, placing maximum emphasis on the practice of sitting itself as the expression of Enlightenment.'
findings.truth: 'Silent illumination' (mozhao) is the Caodong/Soto approach, and it is Soto that treats sitting itself as Enlightenment expressed. Rinzai Zen, described correctly two sentences earlier, works through koans. Naming the whole of Zen as the silent illumination school contradicts the same paragraph.
findings.evidence: Soto/Caodong shikantaza vs Rinzai koan practice; internal contradiction with the preceding sentence

findings.claim: The conclusion and flashcard 9 quote the Buddha's last teaching as 'All conditioned things are impermanent - strive for liberation with diligence.' The body of the lesson quotes it as 'All conditioned things are impermanent. Strive on with diligence.'
findings.truth: The Pali (vayadhamma sankhara appamadena sampadetha) renders as 'strive on with diligence' / 'strive with earnestness'. 'Strive for liberation' is not in the text. The two versions inside one lesson cannot both be a quotation; align to the standard rendering already used in the body.
findings.evidence: accesstoinsight.org DN 16 (Vajira/Story): 'All compounded things are subject to vanish. Strive with earnestness.'

findings.truth: The lesson body, the exam tip, practice question 1 and knowledge check 1 all state that Wesak marks the birth, Enlightenment and parinibbana on one day. The heading names only one of the three and is the exact error the exam tip warns against.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction; spec 3.1.1.2 lists Wesak under festivals with celebrations, origins and significance

findings.claim: 'most Theravada Buddhists extend it to avoiding unnecessary harm to all sentient beings. This is why vegetarianism is widespread among Buddhists... In Tibetan and Japanese Buddhist traditions, meat-eating has historically been more acceptable; Mahayana texts are generally stronger in recommending a plant-based diet.'
findings.truth: The attribution is reversed and the paragraph contradicts itself. Theravada monastics accept meat that is offered under the three-fold rule, and Theravada countries are not notably vegetarian; Chinese Mahayana monasticism is the strongly vegetarian tradition, while Tibet and Japan (both Mahayana) accept meat.
findings.evidence: Theravada three-fold rule (Jivaka Sutta, MN 55); Chinese Mahayana monastic vegetarianism; internal contradiction within the paragraph

findings.claim: The Six Perfections key fact mixes languages: 'Patience (khanti)' and 'Energy/Diligence (viriya)' are Pali, while 'Meditation (dhyana)', 'Wisdom (prajna)' and 'paramitas' in the same list are Sanskrit. The Pali forms are repeated in the glossary and in two flashcards.
findings.truth: The Six Perfections are a Mahayana teaching normally given in Sanskrit: dana, sila, kshanti, virya, dhyana, prajna. Option A: switch khanti to kshanti and viriya to virya across content_html, glossary_terms and flashcard_questions in this lesson, so one list uses one language. Option B: leave it - both forms are correct words and the spec names no term at all for the perfections, so nothing is mark-affecting. Recommendation: Option A, because the list already reads as Sanskrit and mixed forms teach a wrong pairing.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia Paramita: Pali khanti / viriya vs Sanskrit ksanti / virya; spec 3.1.1.2 lists the six perfections in English only
findings.ruling: Leave: transliteration mix is not mark-affecting; spec names the perfections in English.

findings.claim: 'the earth-touching gesture (bhumisparshamudra)' is set solid while 'the meditation posture (dhyana mudra)' is two words in the same sentence.
findings.truth: Inconsistent transliteration only; both name the correct mudra. Not worth an edit.

findings.claim: The Japanese funeral panel calls the forty-nine day period 'the end of the bardo (intermediate state) in some traditions'.
findings.truth: Bardo is Tibetan vocabulary; the Japanese term is chuu / chuin. The claim is hedged with 'in some traditions' and the 49-day period is correct, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.1.2 treats Japan and Tibet as separate contexts

findings.claim: Lesson 1 description is 109 characters and lesson 3 is 103 characters.
findings.truth: The house validator limit is under 100 characters. No factual defect, so not edited here; flag for the description pass.

findings.claim: 'Students who name this distinction... demonstrate the sub-tradition awareness that top-band answers require' (also in lesson 4).
findings.truth: Slightly over-stated, but the spec does require common and divergent views within Buddhism throughout, so the claim is defensible and no board wording is quoted. No edit.

summary: Four lessons checked. The unit-wide defect is the prescribed text: Dhammapada 190-191 is cited six times as teaching the Threefold Way of sila, samadhi and panna, when the verses are about taking refuge and the Four Noble Truths. Three lessons also carry a 2-mark practice question, a part this paper does not set. Places of worship, meditation types, funeral rites by tradition, festival dates and all 20 knowledge-check answer keys are correct.
